=== FILE: 3 B's of Hitting [SbJQmJFWXUw].en.txt ===

=== FILE: Be Where Your Feet Are [E_0rRkorp38].en.txt ===

It might be the most underrated skill in all of mental performance. There's a great story about the Zen Master, Phil Jackson, the great NBA coach, and the teams that he led with Michael Jordan and Kobe Bryant. And during practice, he'd sometimes blow the whistle. Stop everything. Now the team sit cross-legged, midco in a circle and just breathe. No talking. No drills. Just being. Phil Jackson, two of his great books, sacred Hoops and 11 Rings. He talks about building mindfulness and he talks about how at first players hated it until they realized it was training them to stay in the present moment. Be where your feet are. It doesn't come from tension. It comes from being present. From letting go of what just happened, letting go of what might happen and locking into what will happen on this next pitch, this next play, and trusting the preparation that got you there. So what's your vision as a coach of your team being where their feet are, and how can you remind your athletes to anchor down and anchor themselves into the now?

=== FILE: How To Reflect on Your Performance Like Kobe Bryant [wx5rpQz1kmw].txt ===

 the success cycle that when you run your guaranteed success. Hi, I'm Brian Cain, mental performance coach, in the success cycle, it's three steps. Prepare, perform, reflect. Ask yourself as a coach, ask yourself as an athlete. How much of your time goes into preparation, performance, and reflection? And unequivocally, most people will say, most of my time goes into preparation and performance. The problem with that is that when reflection happens, that's where most of the learning happens. So if you're missing reflection, you don't even necessarily know what adjustments you need to make from performance in preparation to get better for the next performance. Prepare, perform, reflect on performance, prepare, perform, reflect on performance, reflection. It can happen in a lot of ways. One way is you look at video of your performance, and you look at not just the mechanics of your performance and the strategy of your performance, but the body language of your performance, the presence of your performance. And you evaluate off of video, just like you would if you were looking at game tape and you were trying to scout an opponent, you gotta scout yourself, the self scout. It's a great way to assess yourself on video. Second way to assess is to simply do what's called a well-better how or a start, stop, continue. When the competition is over, maybe before you take the uniform off in the locker room before you take a shower to wash off the day, you can reflect by writing down, what did I do well? What do I want to do better the next time? How am I going to do that? Lewis Howe is in his podcast in the School of Greatness featured a clip with Kobe Bryant talking about how after every game you have to process it the same way, whether you win or you lose, and you ask yourself, what did I do well? What do I want to do better? How am I going to do the things that I did well again? And how do I do the things I want to do better, better moving forward? So Kobe Bryant, one of the greatest of all time, using a well-better how process to reflect on performance, whether he won or whether he lost. You see, the outcome of the performance is neutral until you label it as good or bad. Now the winner loss is dictated by the scoreboard, but we don't win or lose, we win or learn. And the way that we learn is we do reflection, a piece that most often gets stepped over or mistaken. So the reflection can be the well-better how or start, stop, continue. For example, after a game, a post game, some of the best coaches I've been around, I've seen them take their team and their team would get into smaller groups and do a start, stop, continue based off maybe their position, or based off a certain aspect of the game, like DOC, Defense, Offense, Culture. The coach would come back with a team and say, defensively, start, stop, continue. Offensively, start, stop, continue, culture. And they would process it that way, being player led, instead of it being coach fed all the time. So the well-better how, the start, stop, continue process, those are ways for you to reflect and really extract that learning that you can from performance to allow you to then have more specific and better preparation moving forward so that ideally your performances continue to get better. So understand the three step success cycle. Prepare, perform, and then reflect. So you learn from that performance and can use that in the next cycle of preparation. With the worksheet that's below, I encourage you to go through the reflection process of well-better how and start, stop, continue from the recent performance, generate a discussion with your team about what you can learn, both individually and collectively as a group. You can do a reflection on your own performance, on your team performance, and then collaborate together so that you can learn and make that next cycle of preparation that much more specific and that much better so you can help your next performance.

And holding onto that club as an example of me holding onto that last shot. He was able to let that shot go and play free. One shot at a time. You see every hole, same sequence. He began to recognize the emotional tells in his body, a clinched jaw, a shallow breath, the way he would talk to himself, and he'd be able to reset as he was walking before he got to the next shot. And before that emotional response derailed him, the thing that he learned was to respond to his response. And that makes all the difference. And that's awareness in action. Recognizing when you've drifted. Choose to lock it back in. You see, focus on the other hand, is your ability to aim that awareness intentionally. Picture a flashlight awareness is the light itself. Focus is where you aim it. Too many athletes, they scatter their beam across everything. That they can't control the opponents, referees, the results, the future, the great ones, they, they narrow it down to what they can control, their breath, their body language, their focus, self-talk in the next play. So as a coach, teaching awareness and focus is about repetition and routine. Let's start every session that we have with our athletes with an intentional reset to be grounded in where our feet are. End every game with a reflection question. Every practice. What did we learn today? Because in life, there's winners and learners, and those who will learn will improve their focus and awareness and give them the best chance for success. So how can you, as a coach, build reset reps into your practice? Into your training? So your athletes can train focus, not just their physical skills.

become things the story of roger bannister on may 6 1954 roger bannister a british medical student and avid runner did the previously unimaginable from the start of archiving world records and modern time keeping and track events no one had been able to break the seemingly impassable barrier of the four-minute mile his story demonstrates the prophecy of thought and the power of positive belief at the age of 25 the british sports media had already discovered banister who'd become one of the most scrutinized track athletes in the united kingdom his speed in the mile and 1500 meter events drew initial attention to his talent but when he declined the 1948 olympics in london to concentrate on his training and medical studies he drew the criticism of british track enthusiasts in 1951 banister won the british title in the mile but his fourth place finish in the 1 500 meter race at the 1952 olympics in helsinki the result of a last minute schedule change that compromised banister's preparation routines fueled further scrutiny for his unconventional training regimen after the media publicized his olympic performance as a failure bannister resolved to redeem himself by breaking the seemingly unbreakable four-minute mile barrier he increased the intensity of his training but not the duration and saw steady improvements in his times all while he continued to be a full-time medical student in fact the duration of his training was less than an hour per day because he wanted to focus on his study of neurology banister however was committed to his new goal and loyal to the process he felt would get him there he was convinced that as long as he would continue to see gradual improvements in his times he would maintain his own training regimen the opportunity banister had seconds the unbreakable record had been broken and roger bannister had made history he had made the impossible possible defeating limiting beliefs the four-minute mile story however is not simply the first prayer that ever hit me this is Brian Kane with a mental performance daily podcast and I remember when I was back in junior high in high school I was dealing with some difficulties on the home front dealing with some adversity and I came across a prayer I can't exactly remember where it came from but the prayer you now know is the serenity prayer and at the time I didn't realize how important this prayer would be for me and my life as a mental performance coach in continuing to help myself and my clients get back to Simply what they can control and let go of what they can't now the prayer says God grant me the serenity to accept the things I cannot change courage to change the things I can and the wisdom to know the difference so my invitation to you today is to just accept the things that you cannot change what you cannot control you can't control the past you can learn from it you can't control the future you can influence it and you have to have the courage to do what you can do with what you can control to influence the behaviors that you can control to influence the actions that you can control but you've got to have the wisdom to know the difference so one of the foundational number one things that you can do as an elite performer is to take a piece of paper draw a line down the center write down what I can control what I can't control and make a list and when I've done that with athletes it's amazing how it refocuses them how it gives them a little checkup from the neck up to get back to what's going to help them to be productive because to invest your time and your energy into trying to influence things that you cannot control it's a waste of time the best way to get the things that you want that you cannot control is to go all in on the things that you can control but you've got to have the wisdom to know the difference dominate the day

=== FILE: The One Formula That Will Make Or Break Your Career [_iSb1CNIYyw].txt ===

 the number one mistake that I see coaches allow their athletes to make that sabotages their performance. Hi, I'm Brian Kain. Here's a simple equation that you can use with your clients and athletes to help them move on from adversity, move on from success and get back to where the magic happens, which is in the present moment. Look, yesterday's history, tomorrow that's a mystery, today's a gift, that's why we call it the present. The biggest mistake that I see athletes make is they get stuck on events. Look, win a game, that's an event, lose a game, that's an event, break up with your significant other, that's an event, get injured, that's an event. How are you going to respond to that adversity? That's where we have to get. We have to move past the events that have happened into what our response is because it's that response that we intentionally choose, that we coach our clients through that's going to impact the outcome. E plus R equals O. Event plus response equals outcome. Look at the events that are happening to your clients. How much time do you hear them complain? They're complaining or getting defensive or getting stuck on things that have happened in the past instead of looking at what's my next best decision. The great Harvey Dorfman, a mental performance coach, a mentor of mine said, Caner, there's only three steps that clients should be using to reflect. What was I trying to do? What happened? What's my next best decision? So, ask yourself, what was I trying to do? What happened? What's my next best decision? That's going to allow you to move from the event that's happened that's already over, whether it's a minute ago or a month ago, it's over. Get on to the next play. Get on to the next task. What's your response going to be? Is your response going to be, what was me? Get bitter? Or is it going to be, now we go, get better? Is it here we go again? Now we go. Get frustrated, get fascinated. Get bitter, get better. That response is within your control. Once the event happens and it's done, it's out of your control. And here's the thing. Every event that happens is truly neutral until you label it otherwise. So you have to stay in control of yourself so you can control your performance and you've got to realize every event is neutral until you give it a label. Every event is neutral until you determine otherwise. And as soon as that event happens, success, adversity, anything along that spectrum, get on to the response. And there's only two types of responses. There's responses that we would call above the line responses. They're intentional. They're disciplined. They're winning responses. And then there's below the line responses. They're unintentional. They're undisciplined and they're losing responses. So for example, in the moment you take a pitch, you think it's a ball, umpire calls it a strike. Above the line response, you step out and release. You remind yourself you're not that bad that you need every pitch to win. You get back in the box, fully present, locked in on winning the next pitch. Below the line response, you take the pitch, don't like the umpire's call. You look back, you go palms up, you tell the world what was me, feel sorry for myself. And I'm that bad that I need every call to go my way in order for me to have a chance to win. You're not that bad. So your response has to be intentional. Now, as we choose that above the line response, we also have to practice it. I remember working with the TCU baseball program and at the time they're great coach Jim Schloss Nangle. We were down in San Diego, getting ready to play San Diego State and they had a pitcher named Steven Strasberg, maybe the greatest college pitcher ever. We knew he was going to average about 15 strikeouts plus. So the day before we played, what did we do? We actually practiced striking out and walking back to the dugout with our hand on the barrel, big body language and our head up, sending a positive message about competitiveness to the guy who was walking to home plate after us. We might even have made eye contact looking out the mount at the mound at that pitcher to remind him, Hey, you might have got me this time, but I'm going to be back because what happens otherwise? If you don't practice adversity and you don't know how to handle it, you're going to handle it based off of emotion. And emotion is typically a below the line response. So we have to practice adversity. Like with football players, we practice when I miss a tackle. What do I do to get to the next play? If I drop a pass, what do I do to get to the next play? So you can call that practicing your adversity response or your release routine to allow you to get onto the next event. You see every response that you take though, that's also an event for everybody else. So if I'm a coach and there's adversity, an event, and my response is to throw my hands to get pissed, to get frustrated, to go below the line and cause a distraction. My response is an event for everybody else. Now when the event happens, my response as a leader, my response as a coach becomes that event for everybody else. So can I make it better? Classic example, Braden Montgomery, Texas A&M baseball this year. One of the best players in college baseball gets injured and he's out for the rest of the postseason. What's he do? The next day he shows up, he's in a cast with his ankle. He's got a half that says good. And he helps lead his team from that moment forward knowing that if he's in the dugout, is one of the top pro prospects in the country, one of the top college baseball players in the country, and he's wearing a good hat, that sends a loud message to his team. So it's all at that moment about what's the response going to be. That event is over. A minute ago, a month ago, it's done. What's my response going to be? So event plus response equals outcome. Focus more time on the response, less time on the event that's already over, and you give yourself a better chance to get the outcome that you're looking for.

 I'd say in terms of like specific things that you do in the mental game, what would you say are some of those most specific things that you do in the mental game that help you? I think so far the biggest help for me has been the routines and the processes. And I always knew that a routine was important. I always felt like I had a pretty decent routine, but it was never really structured or detail oriented in the way that it is now. Using things like Habit Share and the Google Calendar to organize my days and give myself that concrete structure. I didn't realize how many things I was missing that I just kind of went in and out of my mind without thinking about it twice. And having those things put down on paper and being organized in that way, I feel like there's a lot more boxes that I'm checking every day. And it also takes that mental weight off of me and feeling like, what do I have to do next? Am I forgetting something? You know, basically my day has turned into wake up and execute. And that has simplified so many things for me and also given me the mental freedom to be able to build on top of what I'm already doing instead of feeling like I'm always fighting that uphill battle. My life has turned into wake up and execute. Love that. Speaking of execution in game, talk about as a pitcher, some of the tools you use like on the mound, whether it be a breath, whether it be three keys to keep it simple, visualizing a pitch. What are you doing specifically when you're out there in competition? Yeah, I think you mentioned the biggest one being breath. You know, that's the greatest controllable that we have on the mound second to probably execution. You know, the breath, re-centered you, realigned you, it resets you. So, you know, that's a great way for me to be able to control myself on the mound when the uncontrollables around me are kind of going astray. And then that focusing on execution. You know, you give up a home run. Okay, well, was it an execute a pitch? If yes, okay, chuck it in the bucket bucket and move on. You know, if not, okay, let's take a look at the process that went into that execution. Was the breath there? Was your timing there? Were the mechanics on? Was it the right pitch to call? And I found myself before I got into this questioning a lot of those things without thinking about if I executed the pitch or not. I threw the pitch that was called and it got hit. Okay, why did that happen? Probably the wrong pitch or probably the wrong timing. And never did I think about like, was it where I wanted it? Yeah, it was over the plate, but was it a quality pitch? Was it a good pitch? And I think that made it a lot easier for me to go in and like fly through a game analysis and a post game report and be like, okay, well, I didn't execute a lot of pitches. No wonder I got hit around a little bit. No wonder I gave up all these cheap hits and two strike counts because I didn't get the breaking ball in the dirt in any of them. And that gave me a lot more clarity on like, what can I work on in my bullpens? Coming out of an outing, things didn't go well, gave up five or six runs, give up a bunch of hits, whatever it may be. You can kind of narrow that down into, okay, I need to focus more on my two strike execution. Talk just about that word of execution, which you used a bunch one executing through the day. I think people understand having a daily routine. What do I need to do? I wake up and execute and knock out what I need to do and then I can be guilt free because I got my shit done. But from a pitching standpoint, execution of just where you can throw the baseball at the end of the day, the only thing that's controllable is where you throw the ball. How important has it been for you to just get fucking clarity of what I can and cannot control? Yeah. You know, there's so many things in this game, especially at the highest level that are not in your control. And it is a mixture of skill, talent, work ethic and a little bit of luck too. Like being in the right place at the right time. You know, sometimes you throw the wrong pitch and it doesn't get hit. Sometimes you throw the right pitch and it does get hit. So having a clear cut, black and white, did I execute or did I not execute? Like I mentioned before, it makes the analyzation part of things so much easier and also the ability to flush it and move on. Instead of hanging onto a pitch and getting into a prayer primal, perfect situation where you feel like you have to do something extra or be somebody that you're not, it makes it a lot easier to say, well, I didn't execute. Okay, next one I'm going to execute. Let's move on. Or I did execute and it still got hit, flush it, move on, keep executing. Love it. Last question for you, Libby. And I think that I choose those two things out of all the things that I could choose because you can't build a house on a poor foundation. And for me, you know, there's been a lot of trials and tribulations that I've gone through playing this game and, you know, it's a lot harder to stay in the big leagues than it is to get there. So I think what I've gone through over the last three years of playing in the big leagues has forced me to really double down on why I do what I do and how much I love the game. And I think if it weren't for those two things, nothing else would have mattered because I probably wouldn't be doing it anymore. And so I think that having that foundation gave me the ability to bounce back the resiliency to keep going when things weren't going my way. === FILE: You can't control what happens do this instead [Q9MlVi1MWEU].en.txt ===

You can't always control the event, the weather, the ref, the opponent, but you can always control your response. And that response determines your outcome. Urban Meyer, he used to post E + R = O everywhere. Locker rooms, team meetings, playbooks. He told his athletes, don't blame the e master your O. He did this leading University of Florida and Ohio State University to National Championships. Author of Chicken Soup for the Soul, Jack Canfield and his book Success Principles also talks about event plus response equals outcome. I once shared this with a high school football team. And one of their players who used to be pretty hot headed and emotional, lose control and get personal fouls, called against him, wrote the formula on his wristband. And then one Friday night after a blown call, a questionable call, I saw him glance down, take a breath, and say out loud, next play. And that's it. That's exactly it. That's awareness turned into self-control. That's the power of this E plus R zero mindset. And when athletes internalize event plus response equals outcome, and they move from the event to the response, they influence the outcome. They stop being victims of circumstance and start becoming creators of results.
